utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. The affirmation you made to tell the truth continues to apply, and Mr. Stamp is finishing his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you participate in any meeting with either Mr. Djordjevic or Mr. Milanovic, or Mr. Trajkovic in respect to the engagement, the original engagement or re-engagement of the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not. Only with Mr. Trajkovic, I had the one meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So the circumstances in which they were -- in which the decisions were made to engage them and to re-engage them are matters which you know only by hearsay being a non-participant?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I heard, I heard from Commander Trajkovic about the reserve force being engaged. I didn't know who was to be engaged precisely. During a regular SAJ command meeting, Trajkovic proposed that a reserve force be brought in. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say when this meeting was?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meeting took place in February.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this early February or towards the latter part of February; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the second half of February. I can't tell you a precise date, but in the second half of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you attend a meeting, a MUP staff meeting, on the 17th of February, 1999, that was attended by the minister, Mr. Djordjevic; Mr. Rado Markovic, the head of the state security sector; Mr. Stevanovic, in Pristina; Mr. Lukic, the entire leadership of the MUP in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a member of the staff, and I did not attend a single staff meeting in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Whether you call it a staff meeting, do you remember attending a meeting in mid-February in Pristina, attended by the minister, Mr. Djordjevic; Mr. Rade Markovic; assistant minister, Stevanovic; General Lukic; do you recall attending any meeting like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, I did not attend a single meeting of the MUP staff in Pristina, and I was not its member. I could not have participated in such meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's not exactly what I asked the last time. Do you remember ever attending a meeting where Mr. Djordjevic, and the minister, and Mr. Rade Markovic were both -- where all three were present in February 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. So these decisions were made at a level above your position, that is what I take your last few answers to mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What decisions do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The decisions to engage paramilitaries and volunteers and groups like the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened without my knowledge. I could not have known or influenced any decisions of that nature, only the SAJ commander could make such proposals. I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If I may show you another document quickly. This is P356. I represent to you, sir, that there was a meeting of the -- a meeting involving the minister, Mr. Djordjevic, Mr. Markovic, Mr. Lukic, the entire leadership of the MUP in Pristina. You didn't attend, but I represent to you that there was such a meeting. And following on from this meeting on the next day, this is a dispatch issued by Mr. Djordjevic. If we could just look at the front. Can you recall if you ever saw this dispatch?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have never seen this dispatch. I can see in the heading that there is no mention of SAJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: One moment. I think I might have misstated something. Very well. If we could go to paragraph 7. Well, first, let's just confirm who sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we go to the last page in B/C/S and the penultimate page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This was a dispatch of Mr. Djordjevic. And if we go to item 7, there was this order issued in respect to compiling lists and establishing control of volunteer and paramilitary units and their members. Did you -- were you familiar with this order?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. This dispatch was not sent to the special unit at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we could move on to something else then, Mr. Simovic. You said that in May, early May 1999, the Skorpions along with the regular SAJ were engaged in activities in Jezerce Planina. Can you tell us where that was? Do you recall the nearest municipal seat to where your activities were? Or where the combat operations were undertaken?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the mountain for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the area of mount Jezerce.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Jezerce Planina; is that the area?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Or Jezerce Planina, or you can say mount Jezerce, whatever suits you best.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where is this? Can you --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kosovo and Metohija. I don't know how to explain it any better, in what area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which was the nearest municipal capital to where this operation took place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can say Strpce.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. In that period of time or on or about the 1st and 2nd of May, 1999, were your units engaged in operations in the area north-east of Vucitrn?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: At that time in early May 1999, were the two side attachments acting in -- together as one unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SAJ Pristina and SAJ Belgrade always took part as a single unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall participating in operations in the vicinity of a town called Skrovna and Slakovci in the Vucitrn municipality in May?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that. We were assigned tasks all over Kosovo; however, at that point in time, my unit was not in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. If we could move on to another topic. I think you said that the commander of the SAJ premises at Batajnica told you that there were bodies that had been buried there, at the 13 May training range. Can you recall about when it was that he told you this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the commander of the SAJ premises who told me. It was Mr. Djokovic, commander of the security squadron of the SAJ. Once we returned there after the war, he told me that at the 300-metre firing range, some bodies had been buried just behind the breastwork.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Instead of squadron it should have been SAJ platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to ask just two questions in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simovic. Thank you, Your Honours. I have nothing further for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Simovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp asked you a moment ago about the SAJ meeting with Mr. Trajkovic and the Pristina SAJ commander. You said that it happened in the latter part of February, you omitted the year though.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had 1999 in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The usher is trying to indicate to you that you should approach the microphone because the interpreters cannot hear you properly.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that it was in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Simovic, tell me this, please, who is responsible for the overall situation and ability of the SAJ unit in order to execute its tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SAJ commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who was that in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was Commander Trajkovic familiar with the staffing levels of the units as well as the level of training and equipment provided?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we kept him always informed, that is to say, Commander Stalevic who commanded the Pristina unit and myself who was in charge of the special unit in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did the chief of the sector, could he [Realtime transcript read in error "we"] have been familiar with the needs of the SAJ unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, unless he had previously been informed by the SAJ commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In your knowledge did Commander Trajkovic towards the end of February 1999 acquaint the sector chief with the needs of the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one of the meetings we had, Commander Trajkovic, Mr. Stalevic, and myself attended it. He did tell us that he informed the chief of the sector about our staffing levels problems and that he had told him we were in need of a reserve force, as well as that Mr. Trajkovic had the people for that. The chief of the sector needed to clear that with the minister, that they be admitted into the reserve force and engaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P1594. Your Honours, page 8, line 16, instead of "we" it should be "he."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, you can see the front page where it says "indictment." The date is 14 April 2008. The document of the Prosecutor's Office for war crimes in Belgrade. The first accused is Zeljko Djukic. Can you tell us whether you can see here if he had served his military service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had. It also says that he is an invalid of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about his previous criminal record, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll up so that I would be able to see the rest of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I don't think there's anything else on that page.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's no mention of any criminal record.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, could we now move to page 2, item 2 of this indictment. Number 2 is Medic, Dragan. What does it say about prior convictions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No prior convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Look at number 3. It says Dragan Borojevic. Can you see whether he had any prior convictions, and if so, in which year?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1996 in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where is Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the next one, can you tell us in which year and where? Do you see the next --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see Miodrag Solaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, not the next name. What are the next convictions for the person we were discussing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Donji Miholjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And where is Donji Miholjac, Mr. Simovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And further below?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says the court in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The court in Vukovar, please. Which year was this conviction?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where is Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: He was sentenced to how many years?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 12 years imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From what you see here, were these convictions made in the presence or the absence of the accused?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1995, all the Serbs from that area moved to Serbia, and many of them were tried in their absence, not because they had committed any crimes, but just because they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did this man serve in the army? Did he do his regular military service?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about Miodrag Solaja, number 4, did he have any convictions, and if so, where and when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2003 he was convicted before the court in Vinkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Will you read it out?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2003 he was convicted by a judgement of the municipal court in Vinkovci, K number 631/03 dated 18 April 2004 for the crime stipulated in Article 177, paragraph 1 of the Criminal Code of Croatia, sentenced to, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, did any of these persons get any convictions in 1999 or for 1999 in the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of them were convicted in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up P40.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We will see on the screen a judgement of the district court in Belgrade K number 1803 against the accused Sasa Cvjetan, dated 13 February 2004. Can you tell us whether this person had any prior convictions? And if so, when?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was convicted in 2001 in Bijelo Polje and in 2004 in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he convicted in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not convicted before 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, can you tell us how the MUP of Serbia checks people for prior convictions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior does the checks through the secretariat of Internal Affairs in the place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who keeps records of convictions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Secretariat of the Interior, they keep them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can the MUP ask for reports for records of convictions outside of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only through the courts, otherwise it cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can somebody's prior convictions be established on the basis of witness statements or citizen statements?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, certainly not. Only from the records of convictions, not from hearsay or statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp showed you yesterday part of the evidence given by General Vasiljevic where he stated that members of certain units had been convicted to multiple years in prison. I'd like to ask you if you had ever seen any document corroborating this statement of General Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen such a document nor do I know of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Has ever a document been shown to you that would indicate when General Vasiljevic became aware of prior convictions of concern members of the reserve unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp asked you yesterday whether members of the reserve unit must have combat experience. Could you tell us what you understand combat experience to mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat experience is understood to mean experience in an actual war, not experience gained through military service because out of 100 per cent of those who served in the army, only perhaps 9 or 10 per cent had combat experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When men are admitted into the reserve force of the MUP, is the regular military service the only requirement?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the law, the person must have done their regular military service and must have no prior convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When the members of the reserve unit came for the second time to Kosovo Polje and when a certain number of them were seconded to you, would you tell me how you assigned them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, I held a meeting with them and based on their military specialty they gained during their regular military service, I assigned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on their military specialty, I formed certain groups that I could use as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me? The microphone is switched on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can't hear counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now we can hear one another. I have here certain documents shown to you by Mr. Stamp earlier. We are all able to read them, I won't show them to you. Your Honours, I have no further questions for Mr. Simovic. Thank you, Mr. Simovic, for giving evidence as a Defence witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, I have a couple of questions, and I would like to take you back to your evidence two days ago, especially to the events in Podujevo. Could you please explain the size of the unit you were the commander of? How many members did this unit have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean my SAJ unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time around 80 men. Between 70 and 80 because one of my platoons remained in Belgrade to secure the base that had been relocated. There were several men who were injured and were absent from the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many of them were present in Podujevo when you arrived in this village?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My entire SAJ unit, I don't know the exact strength, but around 70, 80 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And do you know how many, as you call it, reserve police members were present at that time in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you mean only members of the reserve unit that I brought? Because in the area of Podujevo, there were many reservists who had been seconded to the police station of Podujevo. They also had their own reserve. If you mean the reserve unit of the MUP that I had brought from Prolom Banja, there were two bus loads of them. That means over 100, perhaps 115 or 120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You explained that this unit of reserve police force didn't have a commander. Who was responsible for them? Who could issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were a reserve unit of the MUP, and a reserve force of the MUP is seconded normally to some active duty force. And when that is done, they fall under the responsibility of the one to whom they are seconded. Mr. Trajkovic told me that when I come there, I should meet with Mr. Medic because he was in charge of them. Now, in which way he was in charge of them, whether based on a verbal agreement with Trajkovic or otherwise, I don't know, but in any case, on the orders of Mr. Trajkovic, I made contact with Mr. Medic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, but I didn't understand you. Could you explain again. Those members of the police force, the reserve police force, you have taken to Podujevo. Who on the spot could issue orders to them, to those you personally have brought to Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were brought there, and they were supposed to be seconded to the special unit, the command of the special unit. The then commander, Trajkovic, was not in Podujevo. They were supposed to be seconded to SAJ Belgrade and SAJ Pristina. If I had actually introduced them, absorbed them into my unit, then the commanders of SAJ Pristina and SAJ Belgrade, that is myself, would have been responsible for them. However, as soon as they came, they did what they did, and I just returned them to Prolom Banja. At that time, they were under the command of the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You said that several timings, but in Podujevo when these reserve police force members were present in Podujevo, who could issue orders to them on the spot in this moment in Podujevo? Who was responsible for them? I'm not asking you who was responsible present in Belgrade or in Pristina or somewhere else. On the spot in Podujevo, who was responsible for them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the spot in Podujevo up to the moment they are absorbed, only once they are absorbed into our units then Commander Trajkovic, Commander Stalevic, and I would have been be responsible. Trajkovic was absent. Stalevic and I were there. But they were never absorbed into our units because they had already done what we discussed. They were turned back. I just received an order from Commander Trajkovic to bring them, and I brought them under my authority, but they had by that time not yet been seconded to the command of the SAJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Witness, are you saying that there was nobody present who could issue orders to them in that moment they were present in Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment when they were there, when they were just brought there, and if they had been seconded to us, from that moment of secondment they would have been under our command. They were still undergoing the procedure of admission, but that procedure was never completed because they had done what they had done and at my own initiative and on my own authority, I turned them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you took them to Podujevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And from that moment on, there was nobody in the command of these reserve police force members because they were not subordinated to you? I don't understand that. Somebody must have been in command.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I know and what actually happened. I received from Commander Trajkovic an order to go and get them. At that time they were still reservists of the MUP of Serbia until the moment they are resubordinated, seconded. From the moment of resubordination, they would have been the responsibility of the person who took them over, but the procedure of resubordination had never been completed because of what they had done. They were turned back. They were supposed to wait on the buses until accommodation is found for them, until the procedure of their admission and secondment is completed, and from the moment of completion of that procedure, they would have been the responsibility of the one who accepted and admitted them. At that time they were not responsible to me because I only brought them on my authority and turned them back on my authority when they had perpetrated that crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you didn't hand over them to anybody else, to another commander? You brought them there without turning over them to the command of somebody else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were supposed to be under the command of the SAJ. Since the SAJ Commander Trajkovic was not there, once the procedure is completed they would have been admitted by the commander of SAJ Pristina and myself. However, that procedure was never completed because of what they had done, and I turned them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Some minute ago, you told us that your unit comprised of around 80 policemen of the SAJ unit. How many of them did you ask who was responsible for the crime committed in the courtyard? How many of them you personally asked?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked those who were around on the spot. I mean, the regular members of the SAJ. There were some of my own unit members, there was Dr. Dragan, who belonged to SAJ Pristina, and all of those present I asked if they had seen who had committed the crime. One of my COs Vulevic was also there, and him I also asked. Nobody had seen who had committed the crime. All they knew was that these men were members of the reserve force who had been -- supposed to stay on the bus, but they left the bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I asked you how many of them did you personally ask. You answered those around. How many have been present to whom you put this question?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really at this moment, Your Honour, I can't remember how many. There were several of them, a number of them. I told you how many things happened in such a short time. All the members of my regular unit, I asked all of them. They didn't see. If they had seen, they would ex officio arrested these people on the spot because the SAJ is the most professional unit within the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If you only asked those who were present and around you at that moment, it can't be 80. How could you say that nobody of your unit, nobody among those 80 did see the crime?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the members of my unit were resting. They were in various buildings in Podujevo. Just a certain number of them happened to be on the spot who heard the shooting and ran out. So it was not my entire unit was on the spot. There was just a certain number of them who were around. It's not a large number. I asked all of those who were present out of my regular unit members. They didn't know who had committed the crime. If they had known, they would have certainly arrested the people concerned on the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You told us something about how you secured the site, the crime site. Can you explain that any further, how was the crime site secured?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said I secured the crime scene. I just didn't go there not to trample on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment. I try to find the relevant part. Two days ago in the transcript page 56, line 15 you said: "In order not to" -- you were asked why you didn't enter the courtyard and then you said, I quote: "In order not to trample on the trace evidence. So I was really trying hard, and that's why I went to Podujevo immediately in order to ensure that the site was secured." How was the site secured, and what had you done and ordered?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed the competent authority, and that was the OUP Podujevo, about what had happened. They were supposed to go out to the crime scene immediately and secure the crime scene so that an on-site investigation can take place. After informing the OUP Podujevo, the staff, and General Djordjevic, I did not return to the scene. Instead, I left for Belgrade very soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I take it that you didn't secure the crime site personally, you just informed the OUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All authorised official are familiar with the procedure. They know that after an incident, they are not to go to the crime scene so as not to tamper with any evidence. That is why I only informed the OUP in Podujevo so that they could take measures as soon as possible in order to preserve evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the transcript of the same day, page 60, line 10 and the following, you said, I quote: "That I organised the providing assistance to these people and also to make sure that the trace evidence was not displaced and to secure the crime scene." To secure the crime scene. Again, you left Podujevo with your unit and informed the OUP. How can you say that you secured the crime scene? What measures to secure the crime scene did you take?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of my unit who were on the spot as well as the physician who was there administering first aid, that is what I had in mind when I said that I took care that assistance be provided. I made sure that an ambulance arrived there so that those in need could be transported. When I say that we secured the spot, I meant that my members were there but that no one could actually go to the crime scene so as not to destroy any evidence. That is why I went to Podujevo to inform the OUP there, which was the competent body. They had the necessary personnel such as scene-of-crime officers who were there to properly secure the location pending arrival of investigative authorities. Any authorised official knows that after an incident one should not move about the crime scene so as not to destroy any evidence. This is what you learn in the police high school as well as at any police course. We have the subject called scene-of-crime techniques where the policemen are taught the basic measures so as not to destroy evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'd like to stop you here. That was not my question, what you learned in theory. I would like to know the situation on the spot. When you left the area around this courtyard, the crime scene, who was present from the OUP? Which person was present to be able to secure the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the crime scene for the Podujevo OUP informing them of what had taken place. They were supposed to send out an expert team immediately to do their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you explain how the situation around this courtyard was when you and your unit and the reserve police force members entered the buses and left. What -- how was the situation in that moment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember everything precisely. Right after Podujevo, I boarded the bus and went for Belgrade. I don't know what the situation was at that point in time. I know what the situation was when I left the place though because I left some of my members behind to secure the scene awaiting those from the OUP Podujevo to arrive. However, what the situation was like at the moment I started for Belgrade, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is very interesting that you tell us now that you left some members of your unit behind to secure the scene. That's the first time that I hear it. Can you tell me how many members of your unit you left behind and which orders did you issue to them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said so a moment ago. It was those members whom I had encountered at the crime scene when I went there for the first time. They remained there. No other members. Only those who had been there when I came there before going to Podujevo, the same people stayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: When did they leave? When did you see them again?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. When I left and came back, or?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just want to know when you saw them again after you have left them back?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My members?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about them.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said already, my unit members who were at the location were still there. I went to the Podujevo OUP informing them and telling Medic that he should join the rest of the reserve members on the bus to go back to Prolom Banja. After I arrived in the Podujevo OUP, I no longer went back to the crime scene. Together with my driver, I went to Belgrade. On the way, we escorted the bus boarded by the reserve members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the members of your SAJ unit, where were they at that moment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment they were resting save for a few of them who were still at the crime scene. The rest of them were in our facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked by the Prosecutor if you were the police officer of the highest rank present in -- at the crime scene, and you answered that you didn't see all of the members of the other units and you don't know. Did you try to find out if there's another high-ranked police officer at the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the location where I was and where my unit members were, I was the most senior person in terms of rank. I was lieutenant-colonel at the time. After that, I went to Podujevo. As for whether there were any officials there equal to my rank or senior to me in the immediate vicinity or the general area of the crime scene, that is something I don't know. At that point in time there were regular police in Podujevo as well as the army and special unit of the police, hence I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about the army, but about the police. You said you were the police officer of the highest rank present directly on the spot outside the courtyard where the crime was committed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Another topic, you said that Dr. Markovic tried to assist all those who were injured at that place. How do you know that he could give first aid to all injured people?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment at the scene there were three or four wounded people, that is what I know. Dr. Dragan administered first aid expertly to all of them and ensured that they be transported to the hospital in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How did you know if these 19 people, these dead bodies were really dead or still alive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment I didn't know what the number of people was and whether there were any other wounded among them. I'm only telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You knew that there was a killing at the courtyard and there were dead bodies. How did you establish the fact that these are really -- these people are really dead or still alive?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was informed by my unit members that there had been a crime committed at that location and that there were some wounded people as well as that Dr. Dragan was administering first aid to them, I didn't know what the number of those killed was among the people in the courtyard and whether there were any other wounded. I can only tell you what I recall and what is true to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Simovic, I have a few questions for you, but let me say this straightaway, I fully appreciate that you have been testifying for quite sometime, and I will try my endeavour best to be as brief as possible. But there are matters that I would like you to assist me with. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in the transcript of the day before yesterday, you reported as saying that once the men of the reserve force had been attached to your unit, you held a meeting with them. You said -- you did not identify any of them as being participants in the incidents in Podujevo. Yesterday you said, however, that you did not say "identify," you said "recognise." You said you did not recognise any of the men as being participants in the incident at Podujevo. Do you agree with that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not -- I had recognition in mind the first time around, not identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: My question to you now is this: For you to be able to recognise whether or not the men were participants in the incident at Podujevo, you had to know who the participants were beforehand, wouldn't you not say so? Otherwise, how could you recognise them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I was at the scene and when I saw several reservists there, this is what I meant when I said that I didn't recognise any of them. It's not that I knew that someone had committed the crime and that I wasn't able to recognise them afterwards. I only meant those whom I had seen there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But, therefore -- but if you had seen them and you now would have been in a position to recognise them when you interviewed them; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had I seen anyone committing the crime at the location, I would have detained that person immediately. I said that those from the reserve force who were at the scene who appeared during re-engagement, it is among that group that I couldn't recognise any of them from Podujevo. That was what I meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I'm not following you. You were able to recognise the faces of all those men so that you could have concluded that they were not participants in the incident at Podujevo, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the scene I saw several members of the reserve force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that when they arrived in Kosovo Polje, out of the people I saw there, there were none of those whom I had seen before. Commander Trajkovic did say that the reserve force was to be returned although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- purged of certain members during re-engagement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now, you said you did not look to see the bodies in the courtyard because you did not want to interfere with the trace evidence, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that I didn't want to go to the crime scene so as not to interfere with any evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But your men were moving about there, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several people were there with Dr. Dragan before I came there in order to pull out those wounded. However, when I arrived there, there was no one moving about the crime scene anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But tell me, you did say in the court at Prokuplje that the scene was really crowded with members of different units all mixed together; did you not say that, at the court in Prokuplje?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me explain. At the scene where it had taken place, there were some of my unit members helping. In the general area of the scene in the street and around the houses, there were some other members of the regular police and the reserve police of the OUP. However, at the crime scene itself, there were some of my members, Dr. Dragan, one of my officers, and a few members of the reserve force. This is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So, therefore, when you said "the scene was really crowded with members of different units all mixed together," what scene were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had in mind the general area, not the crime scene itself, but within the perimeter of 20 to 40 metres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, tell me, how long did the incident at Podujevo last? How long did it last?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Time-wise I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: An idea, a rough estimate? Any idea at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very very briefly. When I heard bursts, I went immediately to the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Now then, so you ran outside directly after you heard the two long volleys?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was some 300 metres away. Having heard the volleys, I knew immediately that something unforeseen had happened. I ran outside to identify the direction and move towards there. Some of my members who had also heard those bursts of gun-fire who were closer to the scene ran out too and came to the scene itself. It was my officer by the name of Vulevic and a number of others. When I arrived there, they had already been there at the scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: When you got on the spot, there were members of the reserve force there, were there not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were both my unit members, those of the active force, and some reservists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Right. So there you are, you are on the scene, you ran outside after hearing the volleys of fire, you had this feeling that something bad had happened, and as it turned out, something bad had, in fact, happened. You are also satisfied that the shooting was not done by your men. So did you go to the reservists and say to them, Look here, what is going on, who did this shooting? Did you as a man in authority call for an explanation at all from these men?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who were at the scene -- well, I put a question to all of them and everyone was silent. It was only my unit members who were there, told me, Boss, we didn't see who did this. If they had seen anyone, we would have detained that person immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So are you saying that you also made inquiries of the reservists?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the reservists whom I saw there who were at the scene. This is what I stated in my statement as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Well, you spoke of speaking to your men, but we didn't hear you say speaking to the reservists.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say, Your Honour, that I also asked the reservists who were outside the bus who were on the location who had done that, and I stated that they were all silent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: To this Chamber? To this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was on day one. Perhaps it should be double-checked. I think I said that I asked the reservists who were there what had happened, but that no answer came my way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: It will be checked, thank you. Now then, tell me, Mr. Witness, you said the engagement of the special unit outside the territory of Kosovo was something only the minister could decide, outside Kosovo. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You said earlier in your evidence that the engagement of the special unit outside of Kosovo was something only the minister could decide. But at the same time, in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija from the time the MUP staff was established in 1998, the minister transferred power to the MUP staff so that this staff set up by the minister was able to engage SAJ in KiM without informing the minister. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP staff of the Republic of Serbia -- please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I want to know if you agree or not because I have another question to follow. Now this applied to all the units --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the staff was responsible for all units. It is the MUP staff established by the minister. They were responsible for all the units in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Yes. It applied to all units in Kosovo because the minister set up the staff by his own decision, and this staff had all the power to the minister. Now, Mr. Stamp asked you what you meant when you said, "the staff had all the powers of the minister," and you replied that you were trying to say that if the minister could engage the SAJ outside of Kosovo and Metohija, then the MUP staff was equally able to engage the SAJ in Kosovo. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff established by the minister, the staff to counter terrorism in KiM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: My question to you is this: Were you aware of any occasion when the MUP staff engaged the SAJ without informing the minister?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, oh, you mean the Pristina staff? The Pristina staff established by the minister could engage the SAJ without prior notification to the minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Were you aware of any instance when this was done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the staff issued tasks to all units in Kosovo and Metohija without ministers approval. It doesn't matter whether it was the PJP or the SAJ --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: It happened across the board. Yes, all right. But one thing I would like you to help me with here, and perhaps -- now, the staff could have engaged the SAJ without informing the minister, but chief of sector could not engage the SAJ without the permission of the minister. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the chief of the sector. Who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: I'm quoting what you said. You said the chief of sector could not engage the SAJ without the permission of the minister. Did you not say that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one could engage the SAJ without the minister's approval. No one. Only the staff in the territory of KiM after it was established could do so. Otherwise, outside Kosovo, it was only the minister. In the territory of Kosovo, it was the staff without informing the minister. But also the minister could do it, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You have made that quite clear. Thank you. Now, I'm coming to the end of my questions. I shouldn't be very long. Now you said that during the war in 1999, you and Stalevic did not submit written reports, but upon the completion of each operation, you would analyse the operation together with Trajkovic, and he would then report to the staff. Now, my question to you is: When you and Stalevic analysed the operation with Trajkovic, did Trajkovic take notes of what was being discussed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I said that after each action, after each operation, we analysed the operation, the three of us together. Trajkovic, Stalevic and I. Now, after that, Trajkovic went to the staff. Whether he informed the staff in writing or orally, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But my question is: As you all were there analysing the work, did you see Trajkovic taking any notes at all?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Very well. Was there any reason for you and Stalevic not submitting written reports? Was there a reason for that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not submit written reports, but instead we met with Trajkovic after every operation and made an analysis; whereas, Trajkovic as member of the staff went to the staff to inform them, whether in writing or verbally, I don't know. But during the war, we really did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: But there was no reason for --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no reason. It was just accepted that a SAJ commander -- the SAJ commander report to the staff whether in writing or orally, I don't know. Stalevic and I did not write any reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Whose idea was it not to have written reports?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an idea. Trajkovic as the commander informed the staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: He informed the staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but Stalevic and I didn't. The commander of SAJ Pristina or I did not inform the staff. That was done by Trajkovic who was himself a staff member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: That seems the end of my questions for you, Mr. Simovic. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break now and resume at five minutes past 11.00. It's the first break, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Before we start, I would I like to introduce and ask for permission our intern, Mr. Dobrica Stefanovic, he would like to be present to the trial with your permission, and also, you know other member of the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Familiar faces, but many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we welcome the new intern to your team. He may, of course, be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sit down again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm still unclear about one area of your evidence, and I hope that we can clear that up fairly quickly. This concerns again the members of this reserve force that came with you to Podujevo. I think you told us that it was Commander Trajkovic who had given you instructions to collect this force from Serbia and bring it to Podujevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. On the 27th around 1700 hours when he returned from Pristina, he had been for a check-up at the hospital, then he returned back to the headquarters and came to Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was he then going to go to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he had not been injured, he would not have gone to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On the 27th, was he going to Belgrade after he had spoken to you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After we had that talk, he went to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that for medical treatment or because of the funeral?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He went to organise the funeral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At that stage, the dead member of your unit was still -- his body was still in Kosovo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was transferred from Bradas to the hospital to the forensic department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And do I correctly understand that there were still uncertainty whether the body could be released to be conveyed to Belgrade on the 28th or whether that might have to wait until the 29th for the completion of the forensic examinations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not know with any certainty when the body would be transported to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You went yourself to Serbia to where this reserve force had been assembled; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went to Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was that on the 27th or the 28th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 27th I went on the instructions of the commander to see where they were stationed, that's the first time I saw Mr. Medic and told them that early the following morning between 4.00 and 5.00 a.m. I would come to fetch them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you were able to see Mr. Medic on the 27th at Prolom Banja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him on the 27th when I came to Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you see him on the 28th at Prolom Banja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 28th as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did he travel with the reserve force to Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There were two buses, as I understand you, for conveying this force?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you travel in one of those or in a separate vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was in my car, the car I had arrived in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Medic, did he travel with you or in the buses or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't recall whether he was in my car or in one of the buses. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At Podujevo you left to go to the OUP building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was Mr. Medic with you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was to happen to the two bus loads of the reserve force when you went to the Podujevo building, the OUP building?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were supposed to stay on the buses until accommodation is found for them and then be placed in their accommodation in Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In what way were they told of this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told Medic to tell them not to get off the buses until accommodation is found for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did he do that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you and Medic went into the OUP building, were the men still on the buses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should have been on the buses but it later turned out that some of them got off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When you left the buses, were the men still on the buses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the buses arrived, they were inside the buses. When I went inside the OUP, in the time it took me to get to the OUP building, some of them had got off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where were the buses parked? At the OUP building or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were parked, I don't know at which distance from the OUP building, so that when I went inside the OUP building, I don't know what happened meanwhile. It later turned out that a few of them got off the bus, did what they did, and you know the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You say a few of them got off the buses. Do you know whether all of them got off, some of them got off?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some, not a large number. I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because when I got to the scene, I saw a few of them and later my unit members who were on the spot told me that there were some of them outside the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you see the buses when you left the OUP building?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I saw them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you see whether there were some men still in the buses or not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were people on the buses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, in the OUP building, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Pristina SAJ Stalevic was there, and we were supposed, on the orders given by Trajkovic before he had left Podujevo, to find accommodation for the reservists to absorb them into our units, and after these actions, to report back to the staff. However, in the meanwhile, they had committed what they had committed, and I took the decision to return them to Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You say they -- there was to be a report back to the staff. Is that the staff at Pristina responsible for terrorist action, anti-terrorist actions, or is that the SAJ staff or some other staff?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "staff," I mean the staff for combat against terrorism in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And who was to make that report?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, once we had completed the accommodation of the personnel, then either Stalevic and I would have made the report. It didn't matter who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One or other of the two lieutenant-colonels; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stalevic was a colonel at that time, a higher rank than mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was the time that you were in the OUP building? Are you able to give us an estimate of that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't say with any certainty how much time we were inside because after all that happened, I lost the sense of time. I can't say whether it was half an hour or an hour. I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could it have been longer?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Longer than what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Than an hour?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it couldn't have been longer than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And what was the reason for that delay? Was there some problem about accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was necessary to find appropriate premises where people could be stationed. That place had to be safe, secure. It had to be close so that they are not scattered around. First of all, we had to find that accommodation and then place them, that's why we told them to stay on the buses until they are accommodated. However, in the meanwhile if -- some of them left the buses and after that you know what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Had you found accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in the meanwhile, they were returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What about the task that you and Stalevic had of dividing this reserve force between your two units, had you made any progress with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not have time because they were returned in the meantime. We were supposed to divide them after finding accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Who was looking for the accommodation then?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told my unit members to see if there was any available accommodation anywhere and to report back to me when they find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I take it from what you say that there had been no report back to you about accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they didn't find accommodation. They were only about to look for it because we had also arrived on a territory that was strange to us, new to us, and we didn't know the situation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What did you, Stalevic, and Medic do while your men were looking for accommodation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We gathered in OUP Podujevo. We were not taking any steps yet. We needed to rest a bit, have some coffee, and then go forward with carrying out the instructions of Commander Trajkovic. In the meantime, the shooting was heard and we had not had time to do anything. Immediately afterwards, I made my decision and turned them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What was Medic doing with the two of you, Stalevic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Trajkovic designated Medic as a liaison man with those men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your instructions then had been to go and collect these men, bring them to Podujevo, to accommodate them, to divide them between the two SAJ units, that we've heard. What was to happen to them after that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that if the procedure had been completed, they would have been seconded to us, and if they hadn't committed what they had committed. So if the situation was regular, if there had been no problems, if we had accommodated them, if we had divided them, informed the commander of the SAJ, although he was in Belgrade, and if we had reported to the staff, then they would have become part of the SAJ units. Since none of this happened, I took them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you felt that they would not in any way be part of the SAJ until you had actually divided them between the two units along with the commander of the Pristina unit, they had been accommodated, and you had made a report both to Commander Trajkovic and to the MUP staff in Pristina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Either Commander Stalevic or I would have taken care of that. We would have informed the staff that the procedure of admission had completed. We would have had lists, and they would have been seconded attached to us. However, this procedure never occurred, and you know the reasons. So on the authority that Trajkovic gave me, I as the one who brought them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I stop you because you are going on with a long recitation. I'm asking you, as so many others have done, shorter specific questions and you want to tell the whole story again. Why is it that you considered it necessary before these men became part of your unit or some of them became part of your unit, that they be accommodated, that you have lists, and that you make two reports, one to Commander Trajkovic in Belgrade, and one to the staff in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to inform Commander Trajkovic that I had executed his order. And I would have reported to the staff in Pristina because in the territory of the entire Kosovo and Metohija, that staff was responsible for all units sent there or attached to a unit there, so any unit that had arrived from Serbia to Kosovo and Metohija had to be notified to the staff because from that moment on, the staff would have been responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can well understand that the staff in Pristina needed to know that this force was now in Podujevo and divided between your two units and as it were ready for action, but why is it that a report had to be made before they became part of your SAJ unit and part of the Pristina SAJ unit? What was there about the report that made that necessary?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which report you mean. I just said that once they arrived they were supposed after being accommodated and assigned to units, the staff and the commander had to be informed. However, that did not happen because before accommodation was ever found, they left the buses without anyone's permission, they did what they did, and afterwards, I did whatever was in my power, I actually took them back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm exploring the processes that you have not spoken about. We'll leave the report to the staff in Pristina. Let's go to the report to Commander Trajkovic. Is it your evidence that these men would not have become part of your unit and part of the Pristina unit until you had actually spoken to Commander Trajkovic and reported that you had completed his instructions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If everything had been all right, even if I hadn't been able to reach Trajkovic, I would have informed the MUP staff in Pristina because they were in charge of and responsible for all units in Kosovo and Metohija, because I report to the SAJ commander as my direct superior and then I go on to the higher instance and the MUP staff was above Commander Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to me that it would be a very strange circumstance if you weren't able to reach Commander Trajkovic in Belgrade, say he was around with some members of the grieving family or something, that there could be no completion of the action with respect to the subordination of these men to your unit and to the Pristina unit, everything held up until such time as you could find where Commander Trajkovic was and actually tell him. Do you agree that if you hadn't been able it to reach Commander Trajkovic, you could have gone on and simply reported to the staff in Pristina that you had completed what was required and these men were now divided between your unit and the Pristina SAJ unit?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had not been able to reach Commander Trajkovic, Stalevic and I would have informed the staff that we had executed the order of Commander Trajkovic our direct superior, because he had received instructions from the staff that we may receive the reserve force if everything had been all right. However, since all of that happened, I made the decision to turn them back because I thought that was the most rationale thing do at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we understand each other clearly there. Your instructions that had been given you by Commander Trajkovic were that you were to bring these men to Podujevo, find them accommodation, and with the other commander divide them between your two units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you had sat down with the other commander when you arrived in Podujevo and divided the list of the men in two with each unit to find accommodation, what more would you have needed to do to complete the subordination of these men to your units?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to accommodate them, to hold a meeting, to inform higher levels, and once we had informed the staff to make the staff aware that they were now under our command, that they had been attached to us, and we disposed of them, then that would have been the end of the procedure. So if everything had gone as it had been supposed to, the staff would have been informed and then it would have been considered that they had been attached to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it really that it was because you and Stalevic had relaxed and had a cup of coffee together that this process had not been completed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This process had not been completed because there was a war going on and because of many other circumstances. Another factor that came into it was that we had lost a member just before that. So all the circumstances came together, the bombing, the war, what happened in Bradas. None of those factors played in our favour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let's focus again on Mr. Medic. You mentioned today for the first time that Commander Trajkovic designated him as the liaison officer; is that what you meant to say?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said the first day that Commander Trajkovic directed me to find Mr. Medic, also known as Boca, there, who was the contact person for them, the liaison. So when I arrived in Prolom Banja, I first laid eyes on Mr. Medic, I had a talk with him, the first thing he asked me was, where is Zile, meaning Commander Trajkovic, and I explained what had happened, that Commander Trajkovic had to go to Belgrade, I conveyed the order of Commander Trajkovic that they were to be ready by the next day, and then I returned to Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you go back overnight on the 27th to Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went back to Podujevo, and the next morning very early, I came to collect them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Where were these men housed overnight on the 27th, 28th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prolom Banja is a spa. There is a hotel there. And they were in the hotel of the spa. That's where they were housed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it was to Medic that you turned to ensure that they would be ready for transport early the next morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Trajkovic had told me that he would be there. Now, whether Mr. Trajkovic had spoken to him in the meantime, I really don't know whether he had any understanding with Mr. Medic, I don't know. All I know is that Mr. Trajkovic told me that I should go there on the 27th, and that he would be there as a sort of liaison, and that the following day I should bring them to Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it was Medic, whom you told on the 27th, that the men should be ready for transport the following morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the orders of Commander Trajkovic and in that room where Medic was, there were some other reservists present, so I told everyone in that room that they should be ready early the next morning. I didn't speak to all of them individually to convey the order of Commander Trajkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You say you issued a general order to anybody who heard, or that you spoke to Medic about the arrangements for transport the next morning?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only told them that they should be ready the next morning to board the buses. I also told them that I would be there the next morning to take them over, and I did so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And was it not Medic who was responsible for them to be ready?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medic was only a go-between. To repeat, Mr. Trajkovic told me that Medic was there to liaise with them. As for what kind of relationship Mr. Trajkovic had to Mr. Medic, that is something I don't know. And whether Mr. Trajkovic orally appointed Medic to liaise with them, that's something I'm not familiar with. I only know that the reserve force cannot have an officer of their own. They can only have officers upon being attached to an official unit and then the unit they were attached to takes care of all that such as the issuing of orders, logistics, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is it your evidence then that nobody commanded these men on the 27th or the 28th?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one from the MUP was with them when they arrived. Only the reservists were in Prolom Banja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether Mr. Trajkovic -- well, I don't know that. If Trajkovic had issued orders or had spoken to Medic to be with them pending my arrival, well, that may have been as well, but I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, who was their commander? Are you able to suggest an answer to that? On the 27th and the 28th.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot presume that. I can only say to you what Commander Trajkovic told me about the way to liaise with them. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What about Commander Trajkovic, had he command authority over them?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN SIMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. On the 27th, Commander Trajkovic left the territory of Podujevo having issued the order to me, which I implemented. He told me who to contact, who was supposed to liaise with them.
